description_full: Murphy Oil Corporation, together with its subsidiaries, operates as an oil and gas exploration and production company in the United States, Canada, and internationally. It explores for and produces crude oil, natural gas, and natural gas liquids. Murphy Oil Corporation was formerly known as Murphy Corporation and changed its name to Murphy Oil Corporation in 1964. The company was incorporated in 1950 and is headquartered in Houston, Texas.
ceo_bio: Mr. Eric M. Hambly | President, CEO & Director | Age 50 | Compensation: $2.3M (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 813 people. Revenue per employee of $3.3M ranks in the above the sector median among Energy peers, with revenue falling 11%/yr across its filed history. Each employee generates $279K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $62K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 1× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags moderate compensation governance risk (4/10).
financial_summary: Murphy Oil Corporation is a mid-cap energy business with a $5.3B market cap on $2.7B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -12% over the past three years and -1% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.
Returns on capital run at 8% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business barely earns its keep economically.

The business throws off $227M in free cash flow — roughly 8 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 11.97× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.8× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 3.1×.
Management returns a meaningful 5.5% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 5.7% of the shares.

The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 18% below the high.

Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 4.3% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 4.2% (vs the 8% bar).

growth: Revenue has compounded at -11.6% over 3 years, 6.7% over 5 years and -1.1% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 34%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 39.6% a year over five years.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.0x, 37.5% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 13, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
